title: Recording and Playing Back
bigQuestion: How can a sound, which is gone in a moment, be caught and played again years later?

story.title: Mary Had a Little Lamb
story.kicker: In 1877, Thomas Edison spoke into a machine, and the machine spoke back.
paragraphs: In December 1877, in his laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, Thomas Edison tried a new machine. It had a metal cylinder wrapped in a thin sheet of tinfoil, a crank to turn it, and a mouthpiece with a small needle attached behind a thin plate.

Edison turned the crank and shouted into the mouthpiece. As his voice shook the plate, the needle pressed a wobbly track into the foil. Then he moved the needle back to the start and turned the crank again. Out came a thin, scratchy voice: Mary had a little lamb.

People had never heard anything like it. Before this, a sound was gone the moment it ended. A voice could be remembered, but not kept. Now a voice could be pressed into a surface and played back. The machine was called the phonograph, which means sound writer.

Every record on the Turntables and every sound in the Drum Machine comes from that idea: turn the shape of a sound wave into something that lasts. In this chapter you will follow that idea from wobbly grooves to lists of numbers.
story.think: Edison's needle pressed a track into foil. What do you think the shape of that track had to do with his voice?

lessons.title: The First Machines That Kept Sound
lessons.mainIdea: The first recording machines turned the vibrations of sound into a line traced on a surface.
reading: Twenty years before Edison, a French printer named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville built the *phonautograph*. Sound shook a thin skin, and a bristle attached to it traced a wavy line on paper blackened with soot. It could write sound down, but it could not play it back.

Edison's *phonograph* of 1877 could do both. The needle pressed the wave into tinfoil. Running the needle back over the track made it shake the same way again. The shaking plate pushed the air, and the sound came back out. For the first time, a recording could be heard.

In 2008, researchers scanned some of Scott's old paper tracings and used computers to turn the lines back into sound. One of them, from 1860, is a person singing a few notes of the French song Au clair de la lune. It is one of the oldest recordings of a human voice we can hear today.

words.d: an 1850s machine that traced sound waves as lines on paper but could not play them back
Edison's 1877 machine that recorded sound as a track and played it back

look.title: A Machine That Talks
look.text: Edison wrote that the phonograph could keep a voice, a lesson or a piece of music exactly, so it could be heard again whenever wanted, even after the speaker had died.
look.cite: Thomas A. Edison, The Phonograph and Its Future, North American Review, 1878
look.prompt: What uses did Edison imagine? Which ones came true?

check.q: What could the phonautograph not do?
check.why: It wrote sound waves on paper but had no way to turn them back into sound.

check.q: What did Edison's phonograph add?
check.why: The phonograph could both record and play back.

check.q: How were Scott's 1860 tracings finally heard?
choices: Edison played them on his phonograph
They were always on a record
Researchers scanned them and turned the lines into sound with computers
check.why: Computers read the traced wave shape and rebuilt the sound in 2008.

lessons.title: A Groove Is a Wave You Can Touch
lessons.mainIdea: A record's groove is a long spiral whose tiny side-to-side wiggles copy the shape of the sound wave.
reading: Look at a vinyl record in bright light. You see fine rings. It is actually one very long *groove* that spirals from the outside edge toward the center. Under a microscope, the groove is not smooth. Its walls wiggle from side to side.

Those wiggles are the sound wave, frozen in plastic. A slow, wide wiggle is a low, loud note. A quick, tiny wiggle is a high, soft note. When the record spins, a tiny tip called the *stylus* rides in the groove. The wiggles push it back and forth, the same way the air pushed the microphone.

The stylus is joined to a *cartridge*, which turns its movement into a small electrical signal. An amplifier makes the signal stronger, and a speaker cone moves with it, pushing the air. The wiggle in the plastic has become a wave in the air again. A stereo record even carries two signals, one on each wall of the groove, for the left and right speakers.

words.d: the long spiral track cut into a record whose wiggles hold the sound wave
the tiny tip, often diamond, that rides in a record's groove
the part of a turntable that turns the stylus's movement into an electrical signal

look.title: Following the Groove
look.text: A student looks at a record under a magnifier. In one spot the groove wiggles in wide, slow curves. In another spot the wiggles are tiny and packed close together.
look.prompt: Which spot probably holds a low bass note? Which holds a high sound? Explain using frequency.

check.q: What do the wiggles in a record's groove hold?
choices: The shape of the sound wave
check.why: The side-to-side wiggles copy the sound wave's pattern.

check.q: What does the stylus do?
choices: Rides in the groove and moves with its wiggles
check.why: The stylus follows the wiggles, turning them back into motion.

check.q: Quick, tiny wiggles close together most likely hold what kind of sound?
check.why: Close wiggles mean high frequency. Small wiggles mean small amplitude.

lessons.title: Speed Matters
lessons.mainIdea: A record must spin at the speed it was made for; faster raises the pitch and tempo, slower lowers them.
reading: Records are made to spin at a set speed, counted in revolutions per minute, or *rpm*. Long-playing albums spin at 33 and one third rpm. Seven-inch singles often spin at 45 rpm. Old shellac records from before about 1950 spin near 78 rpm.

Play a record at the wrong speed and something odd happens. Play a 33 record at 45, and the voices sound high and chipmunky, and the song rushes. Play a 45 at 33, and the voices drop low and slow. The wiggles pass the stylus faster or slower, so every *frequency* and the whole tempo change together.

The math is neat. 45 divided by 33 and one third is 1.35. Every frequency goes up by 35 percent, and the BPM goes up by the same amount. A 100 BPM song becomes a 135 BPM song. On the Turntables you can switch speeds and hear this for yourself.

words.d: revolutions per minute: how many full turns something makes in one minute
how many vibrations or waves happen each second

look.title: Record Speeds
look.cite: Standard record speeds; 33 and one third rpm shown as 33.3
look.prompt: How many times faster is 78 rpm than 33 and one third rpm? What would a voice sound like if an LP were played at 78?

check.q: A 33 rpm record is played at 45 rpm. What happens?
choices: Pitch and tempo both go up
check.why: The wiggles pass faster, raising every frequency and the tempo together.

check.q: What does rpm stand for?
check.why: rpm counts full turns each minute.

check.q: A 100 BPM song on a 33 record is played at 45 rpm. About what BPM do you hear?
check.why: 45 divided by 33 and one third is 1.35, so 100 becomes about 135.

lessons.title: Scratching
lessons.mainIdea: Scratching is moving a record back and forth by hand, which plays a slice of the recording forward and backward.
reading: In the mid-1970s in the Bronx, in New York City, DJs were inventing hip hop at block parties. One teenager, Grand Wizzard Theodore, is often credited with making scratching into a technique. He stopped a spinning record with his hand, moved it back and forth under the needle, and liked the sound.

Here is the science. When your hand pushes the record forward, the stylus reads the groove forward, and you hear the sound. Pull it back and the stylus reads the groove backward, so the sound plays in reverse. How fast you move your hand sets the *playback speed*, and that sets the pitch. A fast push gives a high zip. A slow drag gives a low growl.

A scratch is really a performance of physics. Your hand becomes the motor. You are choosing, moment by moment, how fast and in which direction the recording plays. DJs combine this with a *crossfader*, a slider that cuts the sound in and out, to make rhythms on top of the beat.

words.d: moving a record back and forth under the needle by hand to make rhythmic sounds
how fast a recording is played compared to how it was recorded
a slider on a DJ mixer that fades between two sound sources or cuts one in and out

look.title: Push, Pull, Pause
look.text: A DJ holds a record still, pushes it forward quickly for a quarter turn, then drags it back slowly to where it started.
look.prompt: Describe what you would hear on the push and on the pull. Why do they sound different?

check.q: What happens when a DJ pulls a record backward?
check.why: The stylus reads the groove backward, so the recording plays in reverse.

check.q: A DJ moves the record very fast. What happens to the pitch?
check.why: Faster playback raises every frequency.

check.q: Where did scratching begin?
choices: At hip hop parties in the Bronx in the 1970s
check.why: Scratching grew out of Bronx block parties in the mid-1970s.

lessons.title: Pitch Up, Pitch Down
lessons.mainIdea: A pitch control changes a turntable's speed a little, so a DJ can make two records play at the same tempo.
reading: Most DJ turntables have a slider called a *pitch control*. It speeds the platter up or slows it down by a few percent. On many classic turntables, the range is about 8 percent up or down. A record at 120 BPM can be nudged to about 110 or about 130.

Because a record plays pitch and tempo together, speeding it up raises its pitch slightly too. Over a small range, most listeners barely notice. Over a big range, voices start to sound strange. Many digital tools today can change tempo without changing pitch. A turntable cannot. Its sound is tied to its speed.

Why would a DJ want to change the speed at all? Two songs are rarely the same tempo. To blend them smoothly, the DJ has to make them match. That is the next lesson. The pitch slider is the tool, and your ears are the measuring instrument.

words.d: a slider that changes a turntable's speed by a small percentage
a part out of 100; 8 percent of 120 is about 10

look.title: Matching the Numbers
look.text: Record A plays at 124 BPM. Record B plays at 120 BPM. The DJ wants B to match A.
look.prompt: Should the DJ speed B up or slow it down? By about how many percent? What will happen to B's pitch?

check.q: What does a turntable's pitch control change?
check.why: The pitch slider changes how fast the record spins.

check.q: A record at 120 BPM is sped up by 5 percent. What is the new tempo?
check.why: 5 percent of 120 is 6, so the tempo becomes 126.

check.q: On a turntable, what else changes when you speed up a record?
choices: The pitch goes up a little
check.why: A turntable ties pitch to speed.

lessons.title: Blending Two Records
lessons.mainIdea: Beatmatching lines up two records so their beats fall together, letting a DJ move from one song to the next without a bump.
reading: When a DJ blends two records, both play at once for a while. If their beats do not line up, the kicks clatter like two people walking out of step. Lining them up is called *beatmatching*. It needs two things: the same tempo, and beats that land at the same moment.

First the DJ matches tempo with the pitch control, listening in headphones to the new record while the old one plays for the crowd. Then the DJ lines up the *downbeat*, the first beat of a bar, often by giving the new record a small push or drag by hand. If the beats slowly drift apart, the tempos are still a little off.

This is a real measurement task, done by ear. The DJ compares two rhythms, notices drift, adjusts one variable, and checks again. Scientists do the same when they calibrate an instrument. The Turntables let you try it with two decks and a crossfader.

words.d: adjusting two records so their tempos match and their beats land together
the first beat of a bar, the one

look.title: Drifting Apart
look.text: A DJ starts two records together, kick on kick. At first they match. After eight bars, the new record's kick is landing just before the old record's kick.
look.prompt: Which record is faster? What should the DJ do with the pitch control?

check.q: What is beatmatching?
choices: Playing two songs in different keys
Making two records' beats line up in time
Matching the colors of two records
check.why: Beatmatching lines up tempo and beat position.

check.q: Two records slowly drift apart. What does that tell the DJ?
choices: The tempos are not quite equal
check.why: Drift means one record is a little faster than the other.

check.q: What is the downbeat?
choices: The first beat of a bar
The last beat of a song
check.why: The downbeat is the one, the start of each bar.

lessons.title: Sampling: Measuring Many Times a Second
lessons.mainIdea: Digital recording measures a sound wave thousands of times each second and stores each measurement as a number.
reading: A record stores sound as a continuous wiggle. A computer cannot store a wiggle. It stores numbers. So digital recording measures the height of the sound wave again and again, very quickly. Each measurement is a *sample*. The list of samples is the recording.

How often you measure is the *sample rate*, counted in samples per second, or hertz. A music CD takes 44,100 samples every second. That sounds like a lot, and it is. Measuring often matters because a wave that wiggles fast needs many measurements to catch its shape.

There is a rule for this. To record a frequency, you must sample more than twice as fast as that frequency. So a sample rate of 44,100 Hz can capture sounds up to about 22,000 Hz, just above the top of human hearing. That is why the CD rate was chosen. A slower sample rate loses the highest sounds.

words.d: one measurement of a sound wave's height at a single moment
how many samples are taken each second, measured in hertz

look.title: Samples Every Second
look.prompt: Which one can record the highest sounds? About what is the highest frequency the 1987 drum machine can store?

check.q: What is a sample in digital sound?
choices: A piece of a vinyl groove
One measurement of the wave's height
check.why: Each sample is one number measuring the wave at one moment.

check.q: A CD's sample rate is 44,100 Hz. About what is the highest sound it can store?
check.why: You can capture up to about half the sample rate.

check.q: Why must the sample rate be high to record high sounds?
choices: Fast wiggles need many measurements to catch their shape
check.why: You must sample more than twice as fast as the wave wiggles.

lessons.title: Bit Depth: How Fine the Ruler Is
lessons.mainIdea: Bit depth sets how many different heights each sample can have; more bits means finer detail and less hiss.
reading: Each sample is a measurement of height. But how exact is it? Imagine measuring with a ruler marked only in whole inches, versus one marked in tiny millimeters. The finer ruler gives more exact answers. In digital sound, the fineness of the ruler is the *bit depth*.

A *bit* is a single 0 or 1. With more bits, you can write more different numbers. Each extra bit doubles the count. 8 bits can store 256 different heights. 12 bits can store 4,096. 16 bits, used on CDs, can store 65,536.

When the ruler is rough, each sample gets rounded to the nearest mark. That rounding adds a faint hiss or grit to the sound, called *quantization noise*. More bits means smaller rounding and a cleaner sound. Fewer bits means a rougher, crunchier sound, which some musicians love on purpose.

words.d: a single 0 or 1, the smallest piece of computer information
how many bits each sample uses, which sets how many different heights it can store
the faint hiss or grit added when samples are rounded to the nearest level

look.title: How Many Heights Each Sample Can Have
look.cite: Worked out as 2 raised to the number of bits
look.prompt: How many times more levels does 16-bit have than 12-bit? Why might 12-bit sound grittier?

check.q: What does bit depth control?
choices: How many different heights each sample can have
check.why: Bit depth is the fineness of the measuring ruler.

check.q: How many levels can 12 bits store?
check.why: 2 multiplied by itself 12 times is 4,096.

check.q: Fewer bits add what to the sound?
choices: More grit or hiss from rounding
check.why: Rougher rounding adds quantization noise.

lessons.title: The Crunch of a 1987 Sampler
lessons.mainIdea: A famous 1987 sampling drum machine used 12 bits at 26.04 kHz, and its limits gave its drums a gritty sound that shaped hip hop.
reading: In 1987, a sampling drum machine came out that would become a legend. It could record short sounds, like a drum hit from an old record, and play them back on its pads in a sequence. Its sample rate was 26,040 samples per second. Its bit depth was 12 bits.

Those numbers had *limits*. At 26,040 Hz, the highest sound it could store was about 13,000 Hz, so the sparkly top of the cymbals was cut off. At 12 bits, each sample had 4,096 levels, so there was a little grit. Producers also sped samples up to fit more into its short memory, then slowed them down on playback, which added even more crunch.

Hip hop producers in New York loved that sound. It made drums feel heavy, warm and a little rough. Many producers still add grit on purpose to copy it. The Drum Machine on this site copies that 1987 recipe, 12 bits at 26.04 kHz. A limit in a tool became a style. That happens a lot in the history of technology.

words.d: the edge of what a tool can do
a machine that records short sounds and plays them back, often on pads or keys

look.title: Good Enough or Better Than Perfect?
look.text: A producer has two versions of the same drum loop. One is recorded at 16-bit, 44.1 kHz. The other goes through a 12-bit, 26.04 kHz sampler. The second one sounds duller at the very top and a little gritty. The producer picks the second one.
look.prompt: What was lost in the second version? Why might the producer still choose it?

check.q: What was the 1987 sampler's sample rate?
check.why: It sampled at 26.04 kHz.

check.q: About what is the highest sound that sampler could store?
check.why: Half of 26,040 is about 13,000.

check.q: Why did the sampler's limits become a style?
choices: The limits made it louder than any other machine
It was the only machine allowed
Producers liked the heavy, gritty sound they made
check.why: The grit and dull top gave drums a sound people loved and still copy.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Analog and Digital Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Analog recording stores a continuous copy of the wave; digital recording stores a list of numbers, and each way has strengths.
reading: A record groove is an *analog* recording. Analog means the stored shape changes smoothly, just like the wave itself. A tape recording is analog too. Every tiny change in the wave becomes a tiny change in the groove or the tape.

A CD, a phone recording and a drum machine sample are *digital*. Digital means the wave is stored as a list of separate numbers. Between samples there is no information, but with enough samples and enough bits, your ear cannot tell the difference.

Each way has strengths. Digital copies are exact; copy a file a thousand times and it does not change. Analog records wear a little each time the stylus rides the groove, and dust adds pops. But a record can be scratched by hand, slowed by a finger and felt in a way a file cannot. Many DJs today use both: digital files controlled with special records that act like analog ones.

words.d: stored as a smooth, continuous copy of the original wave
stored as a list of separate numbers

look.title: Copy of a Copy
look.text: A band records a song. Version 1 is copied from tape to tape ten times. Version 2 is a digital file copied from computer to computer ten times.
look.prompt: Which version will sound more like the original after ten copies? Why?

check.q: Which is an analog recording?
choices: A music file on a phone
check.why: A record groove is a smooth, continuous copy of the wave.

check.q: What is one strength of digital recording?
choices: It can be scratched by hand
Copies are exact and do not wear out
It has no numbers in it
check.why: A digital file is the same list of numbers every time it is copied.

check.q: Why can a record get noisier over time?
choices: The stylus and dust wear the groove a little
check.why: Physical wear and dust add pops and hiss to analog records.

review.q: What did Edison's phonograph do that the phonautograph could not?
review.why: The phonograph both recorded and played back.

review.q: What in a record's groove holds the sound?
review.why: The wiggles copy the sound wave.

review.q: A record plays faster than it should. What happens?
review.why: Faster playback raises all frequencies and the tempo.

review.q: In scratching, what sets the pitch of the sound?
choices: How fast the hand moves the record
How hard the button is pressed
review.why: Faster hand movement plays the groove faster, raising the pitch.

choices: Choosing two songs with the same name
Counting the grooves on a record
Lining up two records' tempos and beats
review.why: Beatmatching makes two records play in step.

review.q: A sample rate of 26,040 Hz can store sounds up to about what?
review.why: The limit is about half the sample rate.

review.q: How many levels can 16 bits store?
Which statement about analog and digital is true?
choices: Digital files wear out when played
Digital copies stay exact; analog records can wear
review.why: Digital files copy exactly, while grooves wear with use.
